claims.text: Corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel is primarily governed by the temperature-dependent formation and stability of a protective oxide layer.
Aggressive salt exposure over 20–900 °C affects the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
A stable protective oxide layer forms on Q235 steel at higher temperatures.
Formation of a stable protective oxide layer at higher temperatures improves the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
At lower temperatures, the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel is unstable.
Instability of the protective oxide layer at lower temperatures decreases the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
The proposed mechanism applies to Q235 steel in an aggressive salt environment from 20 to 900 °C.
Corrosion rate, oxide-layer thickness, and oxide-layer composition can be measured as responses in a controlled temperature study.
Failure of corrosion rate to decrease with increasing temperature, or failure of a stable oxide layer to appear at higher temperatures, would falsify the hypothesis.
